newsitem.title: USA: Calif. approves PG&E transition charge.
newsitem.headline: Calif. approves PG&E transition charge.

text.p: The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) authorized Pacific Gas & Electric Co (PG&E) to charge an interim transition fee to customers leaving its system, the commission said Tuesday.

The transition charge is aimed at helping established utilities recover some of the cost of power plant construction and power purchases as the state moves from a regulated to an open electricity market.
Before deregulation, these costs were built into the regulated rate structure.

"To ensure utilities recover these costs during the transition..., all utility customers on and after December 20, 1995 - the date the Commission laid out a plan to restructure California's electric industry - will pay a competitive transition charge (CTC) until 2002," the commission said.

PG&E, however, sought an interim CTC from the commission earlier this year when several of its large industrial customers attempted to leave the PG&E system and buy their power from competing vendors.

The interim CTC, to take effect in 10 days, applies to customers "with maximum monthly power demands of 500 kilowatts in any of the two preceeding 12 months who chose to leave the PG&E system," the commission said in a statement.
It added that the interim CTC aims to recover during 1996 and 1997 transition costs included in existing electricity rates.

The interim CTC is to remain in effect until superceded or cancelled by the commission, with payments subject to adjustment on January 1, 1997 and when the final CTC is established, if approriate, the commission added.
Customers committed to buying power from either cogeneration or self-generation units whose construction was planned before Dec 20, 1995, are exempted from the interim CTC.
Customers wishing to leave the PG&E system must notify the utility with 30 days notice.
The CPUC said the estimated overall cost of the competitive transition charge due to PG&E totals about $2.9 billion for 1996, or about 39.2 percent of existing rates.
